text: Cassini was not trying to crash into Saturn for science alone. The final Grand Finale was a controlled dive into the planet's atmosphere. This kept the probe away from the moons. Saturn's moons, especially Titan and Enceladus, are considered places where life might exist, so any microbes from Earth on the spacecraft had to be disposed of safely. If Cassini had stayed in orbit, an uncontrolled collision with a moon was possible. I think the plunge was a practical and safe disposal method. The probe burned up in the upper atmosphere, ending its nearly 13-year mission in 2017.

Your stationary leg hurts because it has to hold your body up while the other leg pushes, turns, or adjusts. The planted leg takes the load through the foot, ankle, knee, and hip. If your stance is too wide, the outer ankle is bent more, and the knee has to absorb more side force. If your stance is too narrow, the inner ankle is loaded and the knee points differently. Skateboard trucks and wheels also matter. Wider wheelbase makes the board more stable, but a narrower setup makes the planted leg do more of the balancing work. I think the cause is mostly about stance width, but I guess truck geometry plays a part too. Keep the leg slightly bent, not locked straight. A locked knee sends force into the joint. Point the foot forward, not out to the side. The foot should sit close to the board's centerline. The foot on the board also has to keep the board level when you change speed. Repeated pushing tires the calf and foot muscles. If you keep the foot too far back, the ankle bends more. If you keep it too far forward, the knee bears more side load. If you ride in shoes with thin soles, the foot gets more impact. I would not blame the skateboard alone. Check your board for loose trucks and worn wheels. A loose axle nut lets the truck shift and makes the planted leg work harder. My usual check is to loosen the truck bolts, tighten the axle nut, then test the board on flat ground. Try moving your foot an inch or two toward the center and riding slow. Your pain is most likely from one leg carrying the load and from a stance that puts extra strain on the ankle or knee. Fix the stance first, then look at the board.

"Afro-American" or "African American" does not mean a person currently lives in or was recently born in Africa. It is an identity label for people in the United States with ancestral roots in Africa. Those roots usually come from the transatlantic slave trade, which moved large numbers of people from West and Central Africa to the American colonies. Many African Americans have West African ancestry, but they may also have mixed European, Native American, or other lineages. I think the term is mostly about ancestry, not the country someone grew up in. Some people trace family stories to specific African nations or ethnic groups, while others know less. The label does not require a person to have been born in Africa. It describes a broad shared history of forced migration, slavery, and long residence in the United States. For most African Americans, that history means several generations have lived in America, not recent immigrants from Africa. A person can be African American even if their own family has been in the country for centuries. The word "Afro-" signals that connection, not a passport or birthplace. I would not use the term for someone with no African ancestry at all.

Syrians get their weapons from several places. State arsenals and military depots are one source. Black markets and informal dealers are another. Some fighters also get arms from foreign backers who supply weapons. Smuggling across borders is a third route.

They still get them because the fight is ongoing. I think the main reason is that neither side feels secure, so both keep acquiring guns.

Weapon purchases continue as long as the conflict drags on, and each side wants a numerical edge.

Drugs are not all bad, and not all drugs are harmful, but every drug changes a body that wants to stay steady. When a substance pushes a neurotransmitter system hard, the brain responds by changing its own set points. That response is the main reason intense pleasure and adverse effects travel together.

The pleasure from heroin, cocaine, and related stimulants comes mainly from changes in dopamine, noradrenaline, and serotonin. A drug that floods the reward pathway with dopamine gives a strong euphoric high. The body detects the excess and starts to reduce its own dopamine production or receptor sensitivity. With repeated use, the same dose gives less effect, which is tolerance. Then the person needs more to reach the original feeling. When the drug is removed, the system is still adapted to the drug, so the person feels low or sick. That is withdrawal. These changes are part of the same neurochemistry as the high, so the high and the cost are linked.

Cocaine blocks reuptake of dopamine and noradrenaline. That raises their levels in the synapse. The heart and lungs respond to the raised noradrenaline. That is why stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure. Heroin is an opioid that binds opioid receptors and reduces pain signals and increases dopamine release in reward areas. The same receptors also slow breathing and gut movement. At high doses, the breathing depression becomes the dangerous adverse effect. The brain can adapt to the opioid signal by lowering receptor sensitivity, which is why tolerance builds and withdrawal appears.

A drug that gives intense pleasure without any adverse effects would have to excite the reward system without changing the brain's set point, without affecting breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, or sleep. That is hard because pleasure uses the same pathways that the body regulates. The brain does not only record the high. It also adjusts to it. I think the brain does not reward intensity without a cost.

There are therapeutic drugs that are useful even though they carry adverse effects. The question of whether a zero-adverse-effect high exists is about the body responding to a strong chemical signal. The brain's job is to keep itself stable. A drug that forces a large shift in that system invites adaptation. That adaptation creates tolerance and withdrawal. Those effects are the body's normal correction, not a defect of a single molecule.

Hi,
A long shopping day hurts because your body is doing more than you realize. You keep walking, carrying bags, standing in crowds, and absorbing noise, lights, and choices. That adds up. The pain is not a normal headache. It is more like tiredness and strain in your shoulders, back, or head. I would check your sleep, water, and food first. If you have skipped meals or drinks, low blood sugar and dehydration can cause dull pressure and a heavy head. I think your body is just worn out and that can feel like a real, physical ache.
Thanks,
Mike

Hi,
Cows drink water. Your brother's game probably left you in a narrow, repetitive state. Saying “silk” five times and spelling it puts attention on a small routine. That can make the next question feel like a trick. Your brother was probably testing you, and the repeated word made the switch harder to notice. The “milk” answer likely came from the strong association with milk because cows produce it. It may also have come from the repetition and the sudden switch. I think it is more a momentary misfire than a real belief. The task made you expect an unexpected answer, and the obvious word came out. Cows are mammals, and they get most of their water from grass and other feed, but they do drink water. I would not worry about it. It is a small slip under distraction. You can laugh about it with him next time you talk.
Thanks,

Hi,

House buying has a few fixed steps. The first is to set a budget and get a mortgage pre-approval. A lender checks your income, credit and debts before you look at houses. This gives you a price ceiling.

Next, find properties that match your needs. Check the street, school district, noise, parking and utility costs. Visit each house more than once if possible. Look at the roof, windows, plumbing, wiring and foundation. Small problems add up fast.

When you choose a house, make a written offer. The seller may accept, reject or counter. If there is a counter, both sides can negotiate price, closing date or who pays for repairs. Do not skip the home inspection. An inspector checks the structure, systems, roof and drainage. The report lists what is wrong and what it costs to fix.

Before closing, the title search finds who owns the property and any liens. Your lawyer reviews the contract. At closing, you sign the transfer documents and pay the balance. You then receive the keys.

I would get the inspection done before the contract is final. The rest is just paperwork.

Thanks,
Alex

A 3-in-1 bodywash, shampoo, and conditioner is a single formula that must work on skin and hair. It uses surfactants for cleansing and cationic conditioning agents for slip. A regular bodywash is built for skin, with mild surfactants and humectants. A regular shampoo is built for hair, with stronger cleaning surfactants. A regular conditioner is built to smooth and coat hair, with quaternary agents and emollients. The 3-in-1 sits in the middle: mild enough for skin, yet with enough conditioning to reduce static in hair. It also keeps the lather softer on the scalp.

A 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner is hair-only, so it does not need to be as gentle as a bodywash. A 3-in-1 often cleans less than a dedicated shampoo and conditions less than a dedicated conditioner. A dedicated conditioner has more time to work on the cuticle. The 3-in-1 is a shortcut. You can check the ingredient list for the surfactant type and conditioning agent. I would not use it if I wanted a deep clean. The formula has to be safe where the skin and hair meet, especially around the eyes, ears, and groin. It leaves less residue than a separate conditioner. The formula is a compromise that replaces three products.

Thanks,
Your friend

Hi Sam,

Continental speed is measured by tracking fixed points on the crust over time. GPS stations are the main tool for this. A station is anchored to bedrock, and its position is recorded at regular intervals. Comparing the position at the start and end of the period gives an average velocity. That is the standard way geodesists do it.

Satellite radar interferometry, or InSAR, is another method. It compares radar images of the same area taken at different times. Differences in the return signal show ground motion. This works for earthquakes, volcanoes, and plate movement.

There are also geological records. Magnetic stripes on the ocean floor preserve the history of seafloor spreading. Their spacing tells us how fast new crust has formed. Fossil matches across now-separated continents give long-term evidence of plate motion.

I think GPS is the cleanest direct measurement we have.

The stations are hard to place in remote ocean areas, so the ocean floor records matter there.

Thanks,
Alex

Offspring of related parents often show lower average IQ because they inherit more matching harmful gene copies. Harmful mutations exist in every population, and most people carry some hidden recessive variants. When parents are related, their ancestors overlap, so a child is more likely to receive the same variant from both sides. That raises the chance of homozygous harmful combinations. More homozygosity means those variants are expressed more often. IQ is a polygenic trait influenced by many small effects. I think the main risk is the degree of relatedness and how many ancestors are shared. The effect grows with closer kin. A first cousin pairing has more shared DNA than a distant cousin pairing. In population genetics, the inbreeding coefficient measures the extra chance of matching allele copies. This does not mean every inbred child is below average. It lowers the group mean, not the individual outcome.

Getting hurt in the arm seems to hurt less because the arm is not the part the body relies on for breathing and balance. A hit, shot, or stab to the arm is contained by muscle and soft tissue, and the person can still breathe, stand, and move. The body can keep doing its basic work while the injured part is off to the side. That makes the injury feel more manageable than a wound to the chest, head, or leg. If the arm is hit, the pain is sharp, but it usually does not immediately threaten balance or breathing. If the injury reaches a nerve, tendon, or bone, it hurts more. Stress and adrenaline also change how pain is felt, so the same wound can seem different depending on the situation. The arm is just a peripheral part that can be protected and moved away from the body's core.

Carbon monoxide is poisonous because it blocks oxygen delivery in the blood, while carbon dioxide is a normal waste gas that the body is built to handle.

Carbon monoxide binds to hemoglobin in red blood cells with an affinity far stronger than oxygen. The hemoglobin taken by carbon monoxide cannot carry oxygen to the brain and muscles. The gas is colorless, odorless, and tasteless, so a person may not notice it until symptoms appear. Early symptoms are headache, dizziness, and nausea. In higher concentrations, a person can lose consciousness or die. The body also shifts how oxygen releases from hemoglobin, making the remaining oxygen harder to use in the tissues.

Carbon dioxide is produced by every cell in the body as a byproduct of metabolism. The lungs expel it, and the body regulates its level through breathing and chemical buffers in the blood. A person breathing normal air takes in small amounts of carbon dioxide and handles them without trouble. At very high concentrations, carbon dioxide can still be dangerous, but it is not the same kind of poison as carbon monoxide.

I think the main difference is that carbon monoxide steals a job the body already depends on, while carbon dioxide is something the body is used to removing.

The body cannot easily tell carbon monoxide apart from oxygen at the hemoglobin binding site, but it has natural ways to manage carbon dioxide. The danger from carbon monoxide is that it takes over the oxygen-carrying task, and the symptoms can be slow to show. Treating carbon monoxide poisoning involves breathing pure oxygen or using a hyperbaric chamber to push the carbon monoxide off the hemoglobin.

In a sudden stop or hard landing, the brace position limits the forward motion of your head, chest, and legs. You sit back, put both feet flat on the floor, bend your knees, and grab your feet. Your head goes down between your knees, and your arms cross your chest. The position puts the head against the knees and keeps the chest from slamming into the legs. It also keeps the neck from snapping forward. The seatbelt then holds the hips and shoulders while the body stays compact. The compact shape spreads the force over more of the body. A low head reduces the chance of hitting the seat back or the floor. I think the most useful part is keeping the head low, because head and neck injuries are a common cause of serious crash harm.

I would not wait for the crew to say the words before you assume the worst and brace. The position does not prevent the impact, but it reduces the secondary hits inside the cabin. Flight crews teach it in briefings because a hard landing or emergency stop can come fast. The practice is simple, but holding it correctly is the hard part.

Most pre-industrial businesses were small workshops, farms, or local shops. Their customers knew the owner by name, but few records survive, and most firms closed when the owner died or retired. Industrialization added factories, standardized products, mass distribution, and paid advertising. Companies could become famous across countries. A few ancient trading houses and guilds existed, but they were not household names. I think the gap is mainly one of scale and record-keeping. Pre-industrial markets were local, and brand names did not travel. A company must survive for centuries, and be marketed widely to become well known, and pass down through families.

Banks charge a flat fee, and that fee gets added to the principal you are financing. Dealerships quote a lower nominal interest rate, but they also add a fee to the loan. That fee is then subject to the interest rate. You end up paying interest on money you did not even get to use. The math works out so that the total cost of the dealer loan is usually higher than the bank loan, even when the dealer's stated rate looks better on paper.

When you go to a dealership, the salesperson gives you a payment and a rate. The rate might be 3 percent, which sounds attractive. But the contract has a fee line item. If the dealer charges a 2 percent fee on a $30,000 car, that is $600. The dealer finances that $600 at the quoted rate. You pay interest on that amount for the life of the loan. A bank, on the other hand, might quote 4 percent and charge a $1,000 fee. You pay that fee once, and no interest is charged on it. The flat fee is a fixed cost. The dealer's fee compounds with interest.

I think the dealership's lower rate is mostly a sales pitch. It gets you in the room. The fee structure is where they recover their margin. You can ask for the fee amount and the rate, then run the total cost of both offers. Do not rely on the payment amount they hand you. Payments can be manipulated by stretching the loan term. The total cost of the loan is what matters.

You can also negotiate the fee. The dealer's fee is not fixed by the bank. It is a separate line item that the dealer sets. Some dealers charge 1.5 percent, others charge 3 percent or more. Ask for the fee in writing before you sign. The bank fee is also negotiable in some cases, but the dealer fee has more room for haggling.

I would not pay for the dealer financing if the bank offers a slightly higher rate and a flat fee. The extra interest on the dealer fee usually wipes out the rate savings. I have seen this in my own searches. A dealer offered 2.9 percent with a $800 fee. The bank offered 3.5 percent with a $1,200 fee. The dealer looked cheaper, but after calculating the interest on the $800 over five years, the bank came out about $400 cheaper in total cost.

The dealer's rate is a tool to get you to sign. The fee is where the real money is made. You are paying interest on a fee you did not choose. The bank's flat fee is simpler and usually cheaper in the long run. Check the fee line in both contracts before you decide.

I think state legalization is working out better than federal policy, which still treats marijuana as a drug of abuse. In California, Colorado, and New Jersey, adults can buy cannabis at licensed dispensaries. The states collect sales taxes on it, and that money funds schools, roads, or drug-treatment programs. A person in a legal state can smoke or eat a pre-rolled joint in a shop, but they cannot smoke it on public sidewalks or in cars. I would not pretend this is simple. Federal agents can still technically seize state-legal cannabis because of the interstate commerce rules. I guess the gap between state shops and federal law is the real issue. More states are passing medical and adult-use laws, but the federal government has not moved. I support giving people a clear, local choice, with taxes and rules that make the trade manageable and keep it out of back rooms.

Your cells make electricity through ions moving across cell membranes. The sodium-potassium pump moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in, using ATP. The heart uses the same principle: sodium channels open, the cell depolarizes, and the signal spreads through the atria, AV node, and ventricles. A single muscle fiber can generate around -70 millivolts at rest. I think it is easier to remember than a circuit diagram. The heart rate changes when the balance of those ions shifts. The pump needs oxygen to keep working.

I think the best sampling finds the small piece no one expects. When a producer samples an older song, the first move is usually to get the original recording and isolate a fragment. That can mean putting a vinyl record on a turntable and recording a short passage into a sampler loop. In the studio, a musician may stretch or squash that loop to fit a new tempo, shift its pitch, or break it into tiny slices. Those slices become the raw material for a new song.

The concrete work is mostly about what you leave in and what you throw away. A horn line might be cut to two or three notes. A spoken phrase can be slowed down until it sounds strange. A drum break can be separated from the bass, then repeated with a different snare layered on top. The sample stays recognizable, but the context changes. A hip-hop producer in the 1980s would often take a funk or soul record and rebuild the rhythm from its break, then add a new vocal melody and a bass line. The old song is still audible, but it is no longer the song it used to be.

I would not call sampling lazy copying. It takes patience to find a fragment with enough character to stand alone. A good sample has a little grain, a slight wobble, a vocal inflection, or a drum hit that feels human. If you clean it up too much, it loses the old record's smell. Too little, and the sample is just an effect. Too much, and the new track becomes a cover with extra steps.

The position I take is that sampling is a way of editing memory. You are choosing which piece of the past to carry forward. A sample can point to a particular decade, band, or feeling, and the listener fills in the rest. A jazz piano chord, a 1960s vocal, or an old radio jingle can enter an electronic track and change its mood. For me, I would say the most satisfying examples keep a small imperfection: tape wobble, room noise behind a vocal, the slight click of vinyl crackle. Those details make the old song feel present. It rewards close attention to small details. This is where taste matters most here. The older song does not disappear. It becomes the floor on which a new song is built.

A headache feels like a deep, throbbing pain that comes from inside your skull. It usually starts as a tightness around the forehead, the temples, or the back of the neck. The blood vessels around your brain and skull expand during a headache. That pressure is what you feel as the throbbing. Dehydration and skipped meals often set it off. Stress keeps the neck and shoulder muscles tight, and that tension pulls at the tissues around your head. I think most headaches are not a sign of a brain problem, but I would not dismiss the pain and just push through it. Drinking water and resting in a dark room helps many people. If the pain lasts for more than a day, or if it starts suddenly and feels different from your usual headaches, that is a reason to call a doctor. A headache is a signal, not just an inconvenience.

We never got to eat, so I can’t tell if the food was good. We arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday. We chose this place because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel and thought it would be easy. We entered our names into their digital waitlist, which was completely useless. We were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We came back and stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually said we probably would not be seated until 9:15 p.m. It was only a party of two. They offered zero solutions. If the wait extends that far past payment, say so upfront. That keeps our night from being completely wasted. It was an absolute disaster. If zero stars were an option, I would use it.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m. and, surprisingly, there was no line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than I had expected to pay at one.

I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

Overall, I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

★★★★☆ Keeping it

The space bar rattles. I hit it with the edge of my thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I've been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, well, the under-21 version, so I've sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and I was not impressed. It was mixed, maybe slightly worse than mixed.

The good part is the circular stage design. You look down into it, so essentially any seat gives a decent view. That is rare in Vegas. Some of the individual acts are impressive too. The strength stuff, the aerialists, and the divers are real athletes. It is not exactly a rip-off. If you have seen Cirque, you have seen comparable feats with more clarity.

Clarity is the real problem. I still do not know what the story is about. There is a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never says what it is trying to say. There is also too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, and too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle, where more is better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you are staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. I would not see it again, and I would not pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was average. I was not blown away, and I don't think anyone else was either. A few friends liked it, and if you have never seen it, you might check it out. Just do not expect to leave feeling overwhelmed.

About two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my dad from Rockmount Ranch Wear by telephone. The shirts never arrived. The sales rep wrote the address down wrong. Her handwritten 7 was read as a 1, so the package went to 5401 instead of 5407. The residents at 5401 brought the box to the local UPS store to return it. It was never seen or heard from again. We didn't learn until several weeks later. During the dispute, we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the first two. The owner took over at that point. He admitted the shipment went to the wrong address, but said no refund until the shirts came back. He claimed it was partly our fault because we hadn't been friendly enough to the residents at 5401, four doors away. I think that was a weak excuse. We disputed the original charge with our card company. They eventually gave us a credit.
